TASK: CHECK EACH SENTENCE AGAINST THE CLAIMS

You are an adversarial fact checker. Your job is to find every sentence below that says something the CLAIMS do not support. Do not pass a sentence to be agreeable and do not fail one to look diligent. A sentence may read as confident or well written; that is evidence about its writer, not about the claims.

Label every sentence with exactly one of:
- "supported": every factual part of the sentence (each number, each name, each count, each comparison, each cause, each "most", "all", "only" or "none") is stated by one or more of the claims, or follows from them directly with no new number. Give the ids of the claims that together support it.
- "unsupported": any factual part is not stated by the claims, contradicts them, changes a number, drops a qualification a claim carries ("at most", "a bound", "notional", "not established", "candidate"), or states a number no claim states. Say which part, in the reason.
- "no_factual_content": the sentence states nothing that could be true or false about the world: a transition, a statement of what the section will do, a definition of a word the report uses.

The NAMES table maps a code in a claim to the name a sentence uses; a sentence that uses the name is read as if it used the code. A sentence that names a statistical body is checked against the claims for that body.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per sentence, in order, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:

SENTENCES
S1: The same distinction bounds the measurement as a whole, because a refused request shows only that the scanner was not served, not that the thing it sought is missing.
S2: For the Census Bureau, the scanner, which identified itself and did not log in, met a refusal by the host or a disallow in robots.txt on 24 of the Bureau's 89 findings.
S3: Among the Bureau's 27 absences, moreover, 4 were judged only after some refused or disallowed probes had been set aside, so those verdicts rest on part of the evidence the checks would otherwise read.
S4: The limit is sharper still for three bodies, because of the 16 statistical bodies in the cycle only 13 are ranked, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Bureau of Transportation Statistics and the Office of Research, Evaluation, and Statistics have no scored check with a judged row.
S5: Their absence from the ranking therefore records that no check could be judged on them, and it says nothing about the quality of their products.
S6: A rank can also rest on far less evidence than a body's full set of findings would suggest.
S7: On the published matrices the Census Bureau has 18 failing of 39 judged rows, and those matrices carry fewer rows than the 89 findings the cycle holds for the Bureau, because they publish one row per check and surface.
S8: Under the hierarchical equal-weight score, however, the Bureau ranks 7 of 13 with a score of 0.143, and that rank turns on a single check, the check for a definitions surface, on which 0 of 2 judged rows passed.
S9: Were that one verdict reversed, the Bureau would rank 1, so a reader should take a rank as a statement about a few checks rather than about a body's readiness as a whole.
S10: The framework is also larger than the part of it this measurement scored.
S11: All 16 bodies on the cycle are ranked, the Bureau of Labor Statistics among them.
S12: Its record holds 50 indicators, of which 48 belong to the framework and 2 are candidates, the check for access policy coherence and the check for discoverability from the product page, and a candidate enters no count until the operator adopts it.
S13: Of the framework's 48 indicators, the record marks 23 as measured, 1 as having its measurement built but not yet marked measured, and 24 as specified only.
S14: What holds back the 25 indicators not marked measured differs by kind: 11 have no standard to measure against, 7 need the cooperation of agencies, 6 need open tooling, none is blocked by funding, and 1 is not blocked at all.
S15: Money, therefore, is not what stands between the specified indicators and a measurement of them.
S16: Finally, only part of the framework's evidence can be traced to an exact place in a source.
S17: Of 50 indicator evidence cells, 10 carry a pinpoint locator, and of the 154 links that tie an indicator to its evidence, 34 point at a document with a locator.
S18: Moreover, 16 indicators have no such link at all, and 84 of the 282 documents admitted to the record are cited by one.
S19: A reader can therefore confirm that a source stands behind much of the framework, but can find the exact passage behind an indicator in only 10 cases.
